strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of current vision-language-action policies: partial observability and temporal dependence in long-horizon manipulation. Maintaining both perceptual and semantic history is intuitive and practically relevant.

The proposed system is clearly organized into retrieval, gated fusion, consolidation, and diffusion-based action prediction components. The presentation and architecture diagrams make the overall method easy to understand.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering more than 150 tasks across SimplerEnv, all five LIBERO suites, and 12 real-world tasks on multiple robot platforms. The reported improvements are particularly substantial on the purpose-built temporal tasks.

Comparisons include several strong recent VLA baselines, and the appendix provides useful task, training, evaluation, and preprocessing details. Component-level ablations support the use of dual memory streams, gated fusion, temporal encoding, and token merging.
Using only a third-person RGB view while remaining competitive with methods that additionally use wrist images or proprioception is an encouraging practical result.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is insufficiently isolated. There is no no-memory ablation of the same backbone, action expert, training procedure, and parameter budget. All principal ablations retain some form of memory, while headline improvements are measured against separately implemented architectures. Consequently, the results do not establish how much of the gain comes from temporal memory rather than the large action expert, training choices, or other architectural differences.

The novelty is moderate. Cross-attention memory retrieval, gated residual fusion, sinusoidal temporal encoding, and similarity-based merging are established mechanisms. The cognitive-science analogy is largely motivational and does not yield a clearly novel computational principle or a substantive evaluation of the claimed verbatim/gist interpretation.

Some comparisons are not fully controlled. Results mix reproduced numbers and numbers taken from other sources, sensory inputs differ across methods, and LIBERO Long and LIBERO-90 are trained jointly, potentially providing additional data relative to baselines. The paper does not clearly establish that reproduced baselines use identical data mixtures, checkpoint selection, action ensembling, and compute budgets.

The real-world evaluation uses only 10–25 trials per task, reports no confidence intervals or repeated-training variance, and assigns task-specific partial-credit scores rather than consistently measuring binary success. This makes several reported differences difficult to assess statistically and makes the term 'success rate' potentially misleading.

Important algorithmic details are underspecified. It is unclear how cosine similarity is reduced for perceptual entries containing 256 tokens, how timestamps are assigned after merging, how independently consolidated perceptual and cognitive streams remain aligned, and how memory is reset and updated during chunked execution. These ambiguities impede faithful reproduction.

The motivating efficiency argument is not validated. A length-256 bank containing 256 perceptual tokens per entry can make retrieval expensive, yet the paper reports no inference latency, memory footprint, throughput, parameter-matched comparison, or scaling analysis versus history length.

The ablations are confined to four relatively short SimplerEnv-Bridge tasks and use only 24 trials per task. They are not performed on the long-horizon tasks where memory is claimed to matter most, and there is no analysis of retrieval quality, gate behavior, consolidation errors, temporal horizon, or robustness to irrelevant history.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the appendix: optimizer and scheduling details, parameter freezing, action normalization, baseline training configurations, validation-set construction, random seeds, and variance across runs are missing. The manuscript also lacks a meaningful limitations and robot-safety discussion.

strengths: The paper targets an important limitation of single-frame vision-language-action policies: temporal ambiguity in long-horizon manipulation.

The perceptual/cognitive memory design is intuitive, technically plausible, and presented clearly, with retrieval, gated fusion, consolidation, and diffusion-based action generation described in a coherent framework.
The evaluation is broad, covering SimplerEnv, five LIBERO suites, two robot platforms in real-world experiments, and several distribution shifts.

Reported results are consistently strong, especially on the custom sequence-sensitive real-world tasks, and the component-wise ablations provide some evidence for using both perceptual and cognitive representations.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not adequately established. There is no memory-free version of the same backbone and action expert, nor comparisons against simple history baselines such as frame stacking, recurrent state, a Transformer cache, or uniform temporal sampling. Comparisons primarily against different VLA architectures cannot show that the proposed memory mechanism causes the gains.

The ablations only compare variants that retain memory. They do not establish improvement over an otherwise identical Markov policy, and they are conducted on four SimplerEnv-Bridge tasks that are not convincingly long-horizon or memory-dependent.

The LIBERO comparison is potentially confounded: Long and LIBERO-90 are jointly trained, whereas several reported baselines appear to use suite-specific training. Access to the combined 100-task training family may provide additional transfer and makes the reported average difficult to interpret as a controlled comparison.

The real-world evidence is statistically weak: most tasks use only 10–15 trials, no confidence intervals or multiple training seeds are reported, and the long-horizon metric awards substantial partial credit. Calling these values success rates and directly emphasizing percentage-point improvements overstates what is demonstrated.

Several important memory details are underspecified. Perceptual and cognitive streams independently select entries to merge, which can destroy their temporal correspondence; the timestamp assigned to a merged entry is undefined. Memory initialization/reset, execution-time update frequency, handling across action chunks, and precise training-time state propagation are also insufficiently documented.

The proposed operations—attention retrieval, sigmoid gating, and similarity-based token merging—are individually standard. The cognitive-science framing does not by itself create substantial technical novelty, and claims that the EOS feature represents high-level cognition or that the bank preserves salient information are not directly validated.

The robustness experiments evaluate only the proposed method, so they do not support comparative robustness claims. Some shifts also cause severe degradation, such as the unseen-camera result falling to 42%.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript does not provide an accessible code or model release and omits details such as optimizer and schedule, frozen versus trainable modules, exact tensor dimensions, checkpoint-selection costs, and complete baseline training protocols. Overall, the promising results are insufficiently controlled to support the paper's main claims at a top-tier venue.

MemoryVLA is a coherent end-to-end design combining perceptual and cognitive memory streams, attention-based retrieval, gated fusion, bounded-memory consolidation, and a diffusion action expert.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: more than 150 tasks across SimplerEnv, LIBERO, and real-robot experiments involving three robot platforms. The reported improvements are consistent across benchmarks and particularly large on the purpose-built temporal real-world tasks.

The real-world evaluation is a meaningful strength. The six temporal tasks test ordered execution, progress tracking, reversible actions, and semantic sorting, where history should genuinely matter; the 26-point gain over CogACT is substantial.

Ablations separately examine memory type, capacity, temporal encoding, fusion, and consolidation. They support using both perceptual and cognitive streams and the proposed gated-fusion and consolidation choices.

The method achieves strong LIBERO results using only third-person RGB, whereas some competitive baselines additionally use wrist-camera and proprioceptive inputs. The paper is also clearly organized and includes useful training, task, and evaluation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not fully isolated. There is no matched full-model variant without memory and no comparison to simple temporal baselines such as frame stacking, a fixed attention window, recurrent state, or history-token compression. Consequently, improvements over largely memoryless VLAs could reflect additional parameters, architectural changes, or access to any history rather than the specific memory design.

Comparison conditions are heterogeneous. Some baselines are re-evaluated, others are quoted from papers or an external reproduction, and input modalities, timestep sampling, model capacity, and training procedures differ. A CogACT-style baseline retrained on exactly the same data and augmented with simple history would be especially important.

The real-world results use only 10–25 trials per task, provide no confidence intervals or multi-seed statistics, and score temporal tasks with custom partial-credit rules. Although the gains are large, uncertainty and full-task binary success rates should also be reported.

Several memory mechanics are underspecified: initialization and episode-boundary resets, gradient propagation through stored states, ordering of randomly sampled LIBERO frames, the cosine-similarity operation for multi-token perceptual entries, and how timestamps are assigned after merging. Independently consolidating perceptual and cognitive streams may also break their temporal correspondence.

The computational cost is not characterized. Retrieving over 256-token perceptual entries with memory length 256 could be expensive, yet inference latency, memory consumption, control frequency, parameter overhead, and comparisons with fixed-window processing are absent.

The robustness section evaluates only MemoryVLA, omits trial counts and uncertainty, and therefore does not demonstrate an advantage over baselines. Performance also drops sharply under unseen camera viewpoints, making the broad claim of strong robustness somewhat overstated.

The cognitive-science framing is intuitive but largely metaphorical; technically, the components are familiar cross-attention, gating, and token merging mechanisms. The contribution is valuable as a system integration, but the algorithmic novelty is moderate. Overall, the breadth and strength of the results slightly outweigh these limitations, placing the paper marginally above the acceptance threshold rather than at a clear accept.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of current vision-language-action models: manipulation tasks whose correct action depends on information no longer recoverable from the current observation.

MemoryVLA offers a coherent architecture combining perceptual and cognitive memory, attention-based retrieval, gated fusion, bounded-memory consolidation, and a diffusion action expert. The dual perceptual/cognitive representation is intuitive and technically relevant.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: SimplerEnv-Bridge and Fractal, five LIBERO suites, Mikasa-Robo, and 12 real-world tasks across three robot platforms. The gains are particularly substantial on explicitly memory-dependent Mikasa-Robo and real-world temporal tasks.

The paper includes useful component studies covering memory type and length, temporal encoding, fusion, consolidation, cognitive-token count, efficiency, retrieval visualizations, and some out-of-distribution and zero-shot evaluations.
The method appears computationally practical, adding only modest reported inference latency and memory overhead, and the manuscript is generally clear and visually polished.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not fully isolated: there is no memory-free version of the same backbone, action expert, training procedure, and parameter budget. Comparisons with separately implemented VLA systems cannot establish how much improvement specifically comes from temporal memory rather than the action head or other architectural and training differences.

Several comparisons mix protocols, sensory inputs, reproduced results, and externally reported numbers. LIBERO averages are sometimes computed over different numbers of suites, while SimplerEnv π0 variants use different flow-matching choices. Exact matched-protocol comparisons with strong temporal-context models are limited.

Results are presented almost entirely as point estimates. There are no confidence intervals, training-seed variation, or significance tests, despite small real-world trial counts and often modest simulated gains. Selecting checkpoints by the best repeatedly measured validation success may also introduce substantial selection bias unless the validation tasks and trials are strictly independent from test evaluation.

The consolidation mechanism is technically underspecified. Perceptual and cognitive streams independently select pairs to merge, potentially destroying their temporal correspondence; the timestamp assigned to a merged entry is not defined; and cosine similarity between multi-token perceptual entries is ambiguous. Memory initialization/resetting, state handling across batched episodes, and whether gradients propagate through stored entries also require precise explanation.

Some claims overstate the tables: MemoryVLA is not best on every Mikasa-Robo task, despite the text claiming this, and it ties rather than exceeds CogACT on real-world Stack Cups. The robustness experiments lack baseline comparisons and often omit evaluation sample sizes, so they do not establish that the proposed memory improves robustness.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the code, model, log, and video entries in the reproducibility statement are blank, while important implementation details such as execution/replanning of action chunks and exact baseline retraining procedures are missing. There are also numerical inconsistencies, including 2,856 versus 2,352 reported Fractal trials.

The cognitive-science framing is largely motivational rather than experimentally validated, and the architectural novelty is moderate relative to existing memory banks, recurrent temporal aggregation, and retrieval-based VLA methods. The work is competitive mainly because of its empirical results rather than a fundamentally new memory formulation.
Real-robot safety, failure modes, and operational safeguards are not discussed, despite deployment of a large learned policy on physical robots.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of single-frame vision-language-action policies: manipulation tasks can require remembering earlier observations, completed subgoals, and action order.

The proposed architecture is clearly motivated and reasonably coherent, combining perceptual and cognitive memory streams, temporal cross-attention, gated fusion, bounded-memory consolidation, and a diffusion action expert.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering SimplerEnv, LIBERO, Mikasa-Robo, two physical robot platforms, temporal-context baselines, OOD conditions, efficiency measurements, and qualitative retrieval visualizations.
Reported performance is strong, especially on Mikasa-Robo and the six real-world temporal tasks, and the component ablations generally favor the proposed design choices.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is insufficiently established because the paper never reports a clean no-memory version of the same architecture trained under identical conditions. Comparisons to separately designed VLA systems cannot isolate the contribution of temporal memory, while the ablations only compare different memory variants.

The real-world evidence is too weak for the strength of the claims. Most tasks use only 10–15 trials, results have no confidence intervals, statistical tests, multiple seeds, or failure variability, and temporal tasks use bespoke partial-credit rules—including loose matching and intent-based scores—rather than strict task success. A few outcomes could therefore materially change the reported margins.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility are inadequately documented. Several results are copied from other sources despite differences in inputs, training, backbones, and evaluation protocols, while the real-world baseline training and checkpoint-selection procedures are not specified sufficiently. Reporting the best validation checkpoint also leaves unclear how selection was performed without bias.

There is no variance or seed analysis for the simulation results or ablations. On SimplerEnv-Bridge, increments are coarse because each task has only 24 trials, so several reported ablation gains amount to very few additional successes and may not be statistically meaningful.

Important implementation details of the stateful memory training procedure are missing: how memory state is initialized, reset and detached; how backpropagation through time is handled; and how state is maintained for grouped or mixed-episode batches. The reproducibility section lists Code, Models, Logs, and Robotic videos but provides no actual resources.

The two memory streams can independently merge different adjacent pairs during consolidation, which appears to break temporal alignment between perceptual and cognitive entries; the treatment of their corresponding timestamps after merging is also unspecified. This undermines the claimed paired perceptual-cognitive history and makes the equations difficult to implement unambiguously.

The technical novelty is modest: cross-attention retrieval, sigmoid gating, diffusion action prediction, and similarity-based token merging are standard components. The cognitive-science framing is largely analogical and is not experimentally validated against simpler recurrent, sliding-window, or matched-capacity memory alternatives.

The generalization claims are overstated. Real-world OOD tests cover only two tasks with no baseline comparison, and the purported zero-shot task-generalization study uses five trials per condition, obtains only 40–60% on the unseen tasks, and again includes no competing method.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of current vision-language-action models: manipulation tasks can be non-Markovian, while many policies condition only on the current observation.

MemoryVLA presents a coherent architecture combining perceptual and cognitive memory streams, relevance-based retrieval, gated fusion, capacity-bounded consolidation, and a diffusion action expert. The method is technically plausible and clearly described.
The evaluation is unusually broad, covering more than 150 tasks across SimplerEnv, LIBERO, Mikasa-Robo, two physical robot platforms, and explicitly memory-dependent real-world tasks.

Results are consistently strong. Particularly compelling improvements appear on Mikasa-Robo and the long-horizon real-world suite, where temporal information should matter most. Comparisons also include several temporal-context VLA methods.

The paper includes useful component ablations, memory-length studies, retrieval visualizations, OOD tests, task descriptions, and inference-efficiency measurements. The reported memory overhead is modest.
The manuscript is well organized, visually polished, and generally easy to follow.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not fully isolated because there is no performance ablation of the same backbone and action expert with memory entirely disabled. Cognitive-only and perceptual-only variants still use memory, while comparisons with external methods conflate memory design with backbone, action head, optimization, and model-scale differences.

Most real-world temporal results use only 10–15 trials and task-specific partial-credit scores rather than binary completion. No confidence intervals, variance across training seeds, or significance tests are reported, so the reliability of some large percentage-point improvements is difficult to assess.

Checkpoint selection uses the best validation step at frequent intervals, but the validation split, number of validation episodes, and separation from reported evaluation conditions are insufficiently specified. This creates potential selection bias.

The consolidation rule independently merges the most similar adjacent pair in each memory stream. This can desynchronize perceptual and cognitive histories, and averaging features may erase rare but decision-critical events. The claimed preservation of salient information is not directly established.

The cognitive-science framing is intuitive but mainly motivational: the correspondence between the proposed modules and human working or episodic memory is not experimentally validated and should not be interpreted as a substantive cognitive model.

Several reproducibility details remain ambiguous, including how recurrent memory states are reset and managed across episodes and batch elements, whether gradients propagate through stored entries, and exactly what the unnamed efficiency-table baseline contains. Released code, model, and log links are also absent in the supplied manuscript.

There are minor internal inconsistencies, including different reported Fractal trial totals and a Spoon-on-Towel versus Spoon-on-Tower task-name mismatch. The OOD and zero-shot evaluations additionally lack matched baseline comparisons.
